criterion_notes.c1: Yes. The paper focuses topically on rural drinking and domestic water supply and access challenges in the United States.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes (broadly), as the paper narratively discusses governmental programs, public versus private utility provision, pricing/cost recovery, and regulatory oversight in rural US water management. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No. The paper does not examine or synthesize any specific rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, administrative burden, tariff rules, disconnection/enforcement, or regulatory structure tested on access); instead, it offers unanalysed macro-governance background, discusses agricultural/watershed conservation subsidies (Conservation Stewardship Program and Environmental Quality Incentives Program), and lists general prescriptive policy and conservation recommendations. (Thus the paper passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 at a topical level, fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, and is excluded under both readings due to the absence of empirical evidence/synthesis in Criterion 3.)
criterion_notes.c3: No. Although the author describes using a PRISMA search flowchart to select 36 documents from 1990 to 2019, the review explicitly mixes empirical and non-empirical sources (including news/blog posts, essays, and conceptual articles), presents no primary data, and conducts no systematic empirical synthesis. The Results section (PDF p. 8) reports only screening counts (65 identified, 36 included) with zero extracted empirical study designs, samples, or effect/mechanism findings, and the Discussion (PDF pp. 8-13) is a narrative policy overview and normative prescription piece. (Note: Table 1 on PDF pp. 5-7, described on p. 4 as listing author affiliations, publication dates, journal names, and impact factors, is blank in the PDF text extraction, while all narrative sections are complete.)
criterion_notes.c4: No. Aside from scattered secondary background statistics cited in passing, the paper neither measures nor systematically synthesizes any household or community water service access, connection, affordability, reliability, or exclusion outcome linked to a governance factor.
criterion_notes.c5: No. Because the paper is a broad narrative policy review rather than an empirical study or systematic empirical synthesis, an analytical unit of analysis, a specific legal/administrative exposure, and a corresponding evaluated access outcome cannot be identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. The full text is written in English (with English and Spanish abstracts).

evidence_quotes.quote: This research evaluates the current stature of rural water supply in the United States putting emphasis on the most significant legal and institutional considerations that hinder water access.
Both empirical and non-empirical sources were chosen with the due basis being drawn on three key factors including:
All in all, 36 documents were identified as suitable for inclusion considering the inclusion criteria defined by the researcher.

Some reflections were found to be articles on this theme and were analyzed through the use of different metrics. Findings from the review process showed that they were effective and could be included in the final summarized information.

Named as the Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP), a grasslands conservation initiative, it provides people living in the rural US with the necessary financial and technical assistance focused on the development of supply schemes for the people (Schultz et al., 2015).

However, the main recommendation is that the government can educate people on how they can develop their own supply systems. In addition, the government has to identify new ways through which they can collect the revenues from private suppliers based on a cost-effective strategy.

raw_response.population_and_sample: 36 empirical and non-empirical documents published between 1990 and 2019 on rural water supply in the United States; no empirical household, community, or utility sample analyzed
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the article frames its literature search around PRISMA and discusses rural water supply in the United States, it explicitly combines empirical and non-empirical documents (36 sources) into a broad narrative policy overview and normative set of recommendations without presenting primary data or a systematic empirical synthesis of study designs, exposures, and access outcomes (c3=no, c4=no, c5=no). In addition, under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it focuses on unanalysed macro-governance background, agricultural watershed conservation programs (CSP, EQIP), and general technical/policy prescriptions rather than empirically examining a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing household or community service access (c2=no). Even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded because it lacks empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Narrative literature review and policy overview (PRISMA-framed search of 36 empirical and non-empirical sources without empirical synthesis)
